name: The Hard Pieces
summary: What a soulstone is, why it is warm, and why an entire economy grew up around breaking open things that cannot fight back properly.
body: Everything that thins gets thinner all the way down and then stops. At the very bottom there is one thing left that will not go any further, and if you break the shape open it falls out into the grass. It is about the size of an egg. It is warm.
This is a soulstone, and it is the only object in Nangijala that is guaranteed not to fade.

It is not a soul. A soul is a whole person and no person ends up in a stone. What is in there is the last piece — one fact, one appetite, one habit of being, pressed down over centuries until it is very nearly a mineral. A thing that spent its existence burning leaves a stone that is still, in some stubborn way, about burning. A thing that endured cold leaves a stone that endures it.

Because a soulstone cannot be forgotten, it cannot decay, and in a world where everything else is quietly going soft that makes it the most valuable substance there is. Work one into a blade or set it into armour and it will lend you a little of what it remembers. It does not make you stronger. It makes you harder to argue with.

One kind of creature gives one kind of stone, and no two kinds give the same one. Nobody decided this. It is simply what it looks like when a particular way of forgetting reaches the bottom, and it means that a stone is a fair record of a kind of creature in a way that a drawing or a description never is.
The people who do this for a living have two words for the work, and you can tell a great deal about somebody from which one they use in front of you.

The polite word is releasing. It is not dishonest. A thing at the stage of Habit has nothing left in it, and the shape it is wearing is going to let go regardless; break it and the last hard piece is saved instead of lost with everything else. Put like that it is a mercy, and a good many people who do it have thought about it carefully and concluded exactly that.
The other word is cracking, and it is what the same people say to each other.

The distance between those two words is the entire moral range of the profession and there is no point pretending otherwise. Everybody carrying a bag of warm stones has made their peace with it in their own way, and the ones who talk about it least have usually thought about it most.

Then there is the rest of what comes off them. Teeth, hide, bone, quills, feathers, cracked stone, a knife somebody was still carrying. Junk, and worth almost nothing, and collected by absolutely everybody.

It is not the material that is wanted. It is that a pile of a creature's leavings is a story with the details still on it — this one had a jaw like that, this one carried a blade of that make — and details are precisely what goes first. Somebody, somewhere, is buying every scrap of it, and has been for a long time, and has never satisfactorily explained what for.
